title: Explain a concept
summary: Turn one idea into a spoken explanation and a visual that makes the relationship clear.
workflow: Use get_rules and list_scenes to identify the audience, existing narration and one idea the viewer should understand. State the learning goal in one sentence.
Write a short script: familiar situation, new relationship, then a concrete consequence. Put proposed narration into create_scene or update_scene so the reviewer can read it in Script view.

Map each sentence to visible evidence, not a second paragraph of on-screen text. Inspect the comparison or process pattern with inspect_pattern when it fits; instantiate_pattern adds a new editable scene.
Use get_scene_html and write_scene_html to adapt the visual to the explanation. Use CSS/WAAPI and data-at word anchors when words are timed; otherwise use explicit authored fallback seconds.
Inspect get_stills and show_scene at the explanation’s key moments. Report what the visual explains, what remains uncertain, and any script that needs approval.

example.title: A rain barrel is a buffer
example.situation: An original explanation for someone new to water storage. No footage or voice is required for this draft.
example.script: Rain arrives in bursts. A barrel stores some of that water. Later, the garden can use it a little at a time.
example.visual: Three labelled cards: Rain → Barrel → Garden. First show an uneven stream into the barrel; then a smaller stream out. Keep the barrel visible across both moments so storage is the relationship, not just three unrelated nouns.
example.tools: Inspect process, then instantiate_pattern with heading “A barrel buffers a burst” and steps [“Rain arrives”, “Barrel stores”, “Garden uses”], duration 10, and the script as narration. Read get_scene_html, replace the generic cards with the two streams if useful, then inspect get_stills. This proposes a draft; it does not claim these calls ran.
example.expected: The viewer can explain why the garden still receives water after the rain stops.

checklist: Does each sentence have visible evidence at the moment it matters?
Can the viewer identify what enters, what is stored and what leaves?
Is on-screen text shorter than the narration, with no unsupported claims?
Have you checked the actual scene and left final narration for script approval?
prompt: Help me explain one concept in this video. Ask for the concept/audience if they are missing. Read project instructions first, inspect existing scenes, propose one learning goal, and map a concise script to a concrete visual relationship. Use this guide’s workflow and checklist. Put script drafts in the video for review; inspect the actual frames and report the result.
guidance: Read get_rules first. Project instructions and the reviewer’s explicit rules take priority over this guide. This is guidance for the chat beside the page, not automatic execution. Read and edit the script in Script view. Do not buy or render final paid narration until the reviewer approves the script word for word. title: Show a workflow
summary: Show what a person does, what changes, and how they know each step worked.
workflow: Read get_rules and list_scenes. Define the starting state, desired result and the shortest path between them.
For each step, pair an action with an observable result. Draft narration in create_scene or update_scene before recording screens.
Inspect process with inspect_pattern for a graphic overview. Use instantiate_pattern for a new scene; replace example labels with actual actions and outcomes.

If the workflow needs a screen recording, do one dry take first. Use existing media only: probe_media, cut_clip, then the returned local video tag in write_scene_html. Never pretend a graphic is a recording.
Use show_scene and get_stills to check the cursor/action, resulting state and a reading hold. Report any missing footage or unverified behavior.

example.title: Name and save a reusable checklist
example.situation: An original generic checklist workflow, represented with graphics until a real recording is available.
example.script: Give the checklist a name. Add the three checks you repeat. Save it, then look for the saved checklist in the list.
example.visual: Action: enter “Before a walk”. Result: the name appears. Action: add Keys, Water, Weather. Result: three checks appear. Action: save. Result: the named checklist appears in the list. Label the scene “Illustrated workflow” when using graphics.
example.tools: Inspect process, then instantiate_pattern with heading “Save a checklist” and steps [“Name → Before a walk”, “Add → 3 checks”, “Save → Find in list”], duration 10 and the draft script. Inspect get_stills. If real footage is later supplied, use probe_media/cut_clip rather than an invented asset path.
example.expected: The viewer sees both the input action and its confirmation; the final state matches the opening goal.

checklist: Does every action have an observable result?
Are illustrated steps clearly distinguished from captured footage?
Does the order match the real workflow, with no hidden prerequisite?
Is the final confirmation readable before the scene ends?

title: Improve pacing
summary: Find rushed explanations and empty holds using the script, scene lengths, audio and timed words.
workflow: Read get_rules and list_scenes. Build a small evidence table: scene id, start, duration, narration word count, audio duration/staleness, narration lead and whether word timings exist.

Compare spoken content and available time. Without audio, label any words-per-minute estimate as provisional, not a measured take. With audio, use the real duration and get_scene_motion word timings; inspect anchorWarnings and sfxWarnings.

Use show_scene and get_stills around suspected rushes or holds. Name a scene-local time and describe what is visible. Do not infer silence from a still or treat word gaps as measured silence without listening.
Propose targeted edits in priority order: shorten one line, simplify one visual, or adjust a reading hold. Explain the tradeoff and keep the reviewer’s intended rhythm.

Apply requested edits with update_scene/write_scene_html. If existing narration audio changes, run fit_scenes_to_narration for those scenes and build_soundtrack when appropriate. Inspect stale audio and lost anchors after script changes. Do not generate paid replacement narration before script approval.

example.title: A crowded 4-second explanation
example.situation: A draft scene is 4 s long and has 22 words. There is no audio or word timing yet.
example.script:
Before: “A checklist helps us remember every small thing we need to check before we leave the house for a walk every morning.”
Proposed: “Before a walk, check keys, water and weather.”
example.visual: Keep three checks visible together after their reveal. Show one check per phrase rather than 22 words of duplicated narration.
example.tools: list_scenes exposes duration/narration/audio. Count 22 words: 22 ÷ 4 × 60 = 330 provisional words/minute, with no allowance for lead or tail. Propose the 8-word replacement, then update_scene only within the requested edit scope. Inspect get_stills and show_scene. Do not claim measured speech or change a take that does not exist.
example.expected: The proposal targets this scene instead of speeding up the whole video; actual speech and reading time are checked before final timing.

checklist: Is each pacing claim grounded in duration, counted words, actual audio or visible frames?
Are estimates separated from measured timing?
Does each proposed edit name a scene/time and the benefit to the viewer?
Have changed narration, stale takes, word anchors and soundtrack timing been checked?
prompt: Review the pacing of this video using this guide. Read project instructions, list scenes, count narration words and inspect available audio/word timing. Show a concise evidence table and at most three targeted changes with scene-local times. Distinguish estimates from measured timing. Inspect actual frames and listen where possible; report limits. Propose script changes for review before any paid narration.

title: Review a video
summary: Give a prioritized review with concrete scene/time observations and an actionable next edit.
workflow: Read get_rules, list_scenes and get_pending_comments. Establish the video’s goal and audience; pending reviewer comments are part of the brief.

Inspect get_scene_html when you need implementation context. Use get_stills and show_scene to inspect the opening, each key explanation and each boundary. Read missingAssets, systemFonts, anchorWarnings, sfxWarnings and stale-audio flags.
For each finding, record scene id, scene-local time (and video time when useful), visible or audible observation, viewer impact and one specific next edit. Separate observations from assumptions.

Prioritize blockers first (missing media, unreadable essential text, incorrect sequence), comprehension second, polish third. State which parts you inspected and which audio/motion you could not assess.

Return a short review with up to three priorities and a checklist. Use add_comment with scene, t and text for requested pinned review notes. Do not mark existing comments resolved or edit scenes unless requested.

example.title: A result arrives before its cause
example.situation: An illustrated workflow scene named save-demo begins at video time 12 s. You inspect the frame at scene time 2.4 s.
example.script: “Save the checklist, then find it in the list.”
example.visual: Suppose the inspected frame shows a success badge while the Save control is still obscured. Report that specific ordering if observed; do not assert it from this example alone.
example.tools: Use show_scene for save-demo and get_stills for its saved version. If the ordering is observed, report “P2 · save-demo · +2.4 s (video 14.4 s): Success appears before the Save action is visible. Reveal the Save action before the confirmation.” add_comment can pin that text at t: 2.4 when review notes are requested.
example.expected: The reviewer can locate and assess each claim, and the next edit has a clear purpose.

checklist: Does every finding name an inspected scene and time?
Are the top issues prioritized by viewer impact?
Does each issue propose a concrete next edit without implying it already happened?
Are review coverage, unverified audio/motion and existing reviewer comments explicit?
prompt: Review this video using this guide. Follow project instructions and pending reviewer comments. Inspect actual frames and available diagnostics, then report at most three priorities with scene id, scene-local time, observation, viewer impact and a specific next edit. Separate observations from assumptions and state coverage limits. Leave scene edits and comment resolution for an explicit request.
